title: The Question
text:
Think about the last few movies you watched. How many featured at least two women whose names you knew? Did those women ever speak to each other? And if they did, did they talk about anything other than a man?
These questions form the Bechdel test. A movie passes if:
The Bechdel test is not a complete measure of whether a movie is good, feminist, or free from sexism. A movie can pass while still portraying women poorly, and a movie can fail despite having complex female characters. Instead, the test captures one specific feature of representation: whether women appear as named characters who interact about something beyond a male character.
This simple test leads to a simple curiosity:
We cannot watch and classify every movie ever produced so instead, we observe a sample and use it to learn about an unknown population proportion (i.e., the proportion of movies that pass the Bechdel test).

title: The Question
text:
The movie sample
To investigate the proportion of movies that pass the Bechdel test, we will examine a sample of 20 movies. Of these movies:

9 passed the Bechdel test
11 failed the Bechdel test.

The observed pass rate is:
\(9/20 = 0.45\)
In other words, 45% of the movies in this particular sample passed. Our goal is to determine what this result can tell us about \(\pi\), the unknown proportion of comparable movies that pass the test.

title: Beginning the Bayesian Analysis
text:
We now shift from asking about data given a parameter to asking about the parameter given our data.
The frequentist analysis told us that 9 or fewer passes would not be unusual if \(p\) were 0.50. However, it does not directly answer the question we may be most interested in:
To make a probability statement about \(p\) itself, we need to represent our uncertainty about \(p\) with a probability distribution. This brings us to the Bayesian approach. Unlike the frequentist analysis, Bayesian inference requires us to consider what values of \(p\) seemed plausible before we observed the sample.
Suppose three moviegoers are asked the following question before seeing the sample:
These people do not begin with the same beliefs. A Bayesian analysis does not require us to hide this disagreement. Instead, each person can represent their uncertainty with a prior distribution.
A prior is not simply one predicted value. It is a distribution over all possible values of \(p\). For example, someone might think that \(p\) is probably near 0.30 but admit that values such as 0.20 or 0.50 are also possible. Another person might place equal prior plausibility on every value between 0 and 1.
The prior makes these starting assumptions visible.

title: Comparing the Frequentist and Bayesian Results
text:
What Could Go Wrong?
Important: The sample pass rate, 0.45 (9 of 20 movies), does not establish the pass rate for all movies.

Small sample. Twenty movies leave substantial uncertainty, so different priors can produce different conclusions.
Teaching priors. Beta(3, 7), Beta(1, 1), and Beta(7, 3) illustrate viewpoints; they are not based on earlier studies.
Sample selection. Some years, genres, countries, budgets, or release types may be overrepresented.
One shared \(p\). The model assumes a common pass probability, though it may vary across time and movie characteristics.
Independence. Movies sharing a studio, creative team, or franchise may have related outcomes.
Judgment calls. Viewers may disagree about whether a movie meets each test criterion.
A narrow test. Passing does not establish the quality, depth, or prominence of women’s representation.
No causal conclusion. This analysis cannot show whether passing changes revenue, reviews, or audience responses.

Allowing the pass probability to vary by year or genre would require extending the model—for example, through regression or hierarchical modeling. That is beyond this introduction.

title: Learning One Movie at a Time
text:
Does the order of the movies change the final posterior?
Bayesian learning can occur sequentially. Suppose we begin with the lower-pass prior:
\[
p \sim \text{Beta}(3, 7)
\]
The 20 movies still contain 9 passes and 11 failures. The order below is one possible order for those same movies. The final posterior does not depend on that order.
The first movie passes. The updated distribution becomes:
\[
p \mid \text{first movie} \sim \text{Beta}(4, 7)
\]
The second movie fails:
\[
p \mid \text{first two movies} \sim \text{Beta}(4, 8)
\]
Each passing movie adds one to the first parameter. Each failing movie adds one to the second parameter.
After all 20 movies, the result is:
\[
p \mid \text{all 20 movies} \sim \text{Beta}(12, 18)
\]
The posterior after one stage becomes the prior for the next stage. Updating one movie at a time produces the same final posterior as updating with all 20 movies at once, assuming the same model and starting prior.
Move through the movies one at a time. The density is the updated distribution after the movies revealed so far. The lower graph tracks its mean, with a band one standard deviation on either side.

title: The Posterior Mean and Shrinkage
text:
After finding the entire posterior distribution, we may want a single value that summarizes our updated estimate of \(p\). One common Bayesian estimate is the posterior mean.
The posterior mean is the average of all possible values of \(p\) under the posterior distribution, weighted by how plausible each value is after observing the data. It can be interpreted as our updated point estimate of the proportion of movies that pass the Bechdel test.
For a Beta(\(a\), \(b\)) posterior, the posterior mean is:
\[
E(p \mid y) = \frac{a}{a + b}
\]
Using the lower-pass prior, we obtained:
\[
p \mid y \sim \text{Beta}(12, 18)
\]
Therefore:
\[
E(p \mid y) = 12/(12 + 18) = 12/30 = 0.40
\]
Based on this prior and the observed sample, our posterior estimate is that 40% of comparable movies pass the Bechdel test.
The sample proportion was:
\[
y/n = 9/20 = 0.45
\]
However, the posterior mean is 0.40.
The Beta(3, 7) prior had a mean of:
\[
3/(3 + 7) = 0.30
\]
The posterior mean falls between the prior mean of 0.30 and the sample proportion of 0.45. It has moved away from the sample proportion and toward the prior mean. This movement is called shrinkage.
In Bayesian statistics, shrinkage occurs when the posterior estimate is pulled toward the prior estimate. The amount of shrinkage depends on the relative amount of information represented by the prior and the data.

title: From Twenty Movies to an Unknown Proportion
text:
Let \(p\) represent the unknown proportion of movies in the relevant population that pass the Bechdel test.
\(p = P\)(a randomly selected movie passes the Bechdel test)
If \(p = 0.30\), then approximately 30% of movies in the population pass.
If \(p = 0.50\), then approximately half pass.
If \(p = 0.80\), then approximately 80% pass.
We do not know the true value of \(p\). What we observe is the sample proportion:
\(\hat{p} = y/n\)
Here:
\(\hat{p} = 9/20 = 0.45\)
The sample tells us that 45% of these 20 movies passed. However, \(\hat{p}\) and \(p\) are not the same thing. \(p\) is the unknown population proportion we want to estimate and \(\hat{p}\) is a statistic calculated from the particular sample we observed.

title: Beyond Pass or Fail
text:
This website is intended for students who have completed STAT 360 or a similar probability course and are familiar with frequentist methods. You should be familiar with probability distributions, random variables, expected values, and basic statistical notation.
You do not need previous experience with Bayesian statistics. Concepts such as priors, likelihoods, posterior distributions, conjugacy, credible intervals, and posterior prediction will be introduced from the beginning.
We will briefly review frequentist ideas such as maximum likelihood estimation, confidence intervals, and hypothesis testing. The goal is not to reteach all of frequentist inference, but to use familiar methods as a bridge to Bayesian thinking.

title: Updating with Bayes’ Rule
text:
Now we reach the central step of Bayesian inference: combining our prior beliefs with the movie data to produce an updated distribution for \(p\).
The general form of Bayes’ rule is:
\[
f(p \mid y) = \frac{f(y \mid p)\, f(p)}{f(y)}
\]
This can be summarized as:
\[
\text{Posterior} \propto \text{Likelihood} \times \text{Prior}
\]
